title: CYBER ATTACKS ON U.S.BASE WATER SYSTEMS INCLUDING MINNESOTA AND BEYOND
executiveAssessment: Publicly available evidence establishes that a coordinated cyber campaign affected operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26-27, 2026 . Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) publicly confirmed the scope, stated that the activity targeted technology used to remotely monitor and control water equipment, and said confirmed cases involved PLCs and HMIs. Minnesota also stated that the state had not attributed the activity to a specific actor as of July 30, 2026. MNIT, July 28, 2026 ; MNIT, July 30, 2026 Federal evidence further establishes that similar malicious activity expanded beyond Minnesota. On July 30, 2026 , the FBI and EPA warned that water and wastewater utilities in at least seven U.S. states had reported incidents since July 27, and that some of the activity degraded water operations. The FBI/EPA PSA identified the affected technology class as internet-facing Rockwell Automation / Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs, and described observed attacker actions: remote access, password changes, IP-address changes, loss of monitoring and control, and at least one report of modified PLC project files / ladder-logic discrepancies. FBI/EPA PSA, July 30, 2026 Confirmed operational impacts varied by victim. Minnesota publicly emphasized that "impacted" did not mean every affected community lost water service. Public reporting and local statements indicate at least some utilities reverted to manual operations; Braham temporarily lost automated operating controls and briefly took its plant offline; Plymouth lost communications to two water towers and several lift stations but maintained normal operations through manual procedures; South St. Paul and Maple Plain reported impacts to automated controls while maintaining water and wastewater service. MNIT stated it was not aware of any active Minnesota requests for residents to modify drinking water use as of July 30. MNIT, July 30, 2026 ; MPR News, July 27-28, 2026 ; City of Plymouth listing, July 27, 2026 The strongest publicly supported methodology finding is that the campaign exploited internet-exposed OT . Both Minnesota and the FBI/EPA urged utilities to remove PLCs, HMIs, and other OT from direct internet access, replace default credentials, require MFA where supported, and review remote-access logs. The FBI/EPA also specifically highlighted cellular modems and remote connectivity architectures. These recommendations align closely with the attack behavior described in the PSA and with Minnesota's statement that the affected technology was used for remote monitoring and control. MNIT, July 30, 2026 ; FBI/EPA PSA, July 30, 2026 Attribution remains UNRESOLVED on the public record for the Minnesota incidents. Federal authorities had already issued Iran-related PLC warnings in April and July 2026, and reputable reporting said U.S. officials were investigating whether Iran was responsible. However, Minnesota explicitly stated on July 30 that it was not attributing the activity to a specific actor, and the available public evidence does not meet the threshold for confirmed attribution. At most, the incidents appear consistent with the broader pattern of Iranian-affiliated targeting of internet-exposed PLCs described in 2023-2026 government advisories. MNIT, July 30, 2026 ; EPA/FBI/CISA/NSA, April 6, 2026 ; FBI, July 22, 2026 Bottom line: The public record supports a defensible conclusion that the July 2026 Minnesota incidents were part of a broader U.S. pattern of malicious targeting of internet-facing water-sector OT, especially PLC-based remote monitoring/control environments. It does not yet support confirmed public attribution of the Minnesota incidents to a named actor.

FBI/EPA PSA At least one organization reported modified PLC project files and ladder-logic discrepancies across several sites. FBI/EPA PSA Minnesota confirmed involvement of PLCs and HMIs used for remote monitoring/control. MNIT, July 30 Across several victims, similarities in third-party-provided network setup may have enabled repeated success where common vulnerable configurations existed. sections.heading: INVESTIGATIVE LEADS
sections.text: Obtain local official statements, council packets, or incident briefings from Minnesota communities beyond Braham, Plymouth, South St. Paul, and Maple Plain. Seek any state open-records releases after investigation closure regarding affected equipment types, modem use, and remote-access configuration. Review future FBI/CISA/EPA updates for released IOCs, named states, and recovered TTP detail. Identify whether specific Rockwell models beyond MicroLogix 1100/1400 were involved in the seven-state wave. Examine whether common integrators, OEM templates, or cellular-network configurations recur across victims. Monitor Michigan, Georgia, South Dakota, and New Jersey public records for primary-source incident confirmations. Check whether EPA water-sector technical assistance engagements or state primacy agencies later disclose anonymized findings.

sections.heading: FINAL ASSESSMENT
sections.text: WHAT DO WE KNOW? A coordinated cyberattack targeted OT at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26-27, 2026. MNIT Most confirmed Minnesota cases involved PLCs and HMIs used to remotely monitor and control water equipment. MNIT Since July 27, 2026, water and wastewater utilities in at least seven states reported similar incidents to the FBI; some activity degraded operations. FBI/EPA PSA The publicly described method involved remote access to internet-facing PLCs, followed by password and IP changes causing loss of monitoring/control. FBI/EPA PSA Some communities switched to manual procedures; Braham experienced the clearest reported operational disruption in Minnesota. MPR News WHAT DO WE ASSESS? The Minnesota incidents were likely part of a broader wave of opportunistic or coordinated targeting against similarly exposed water-sector OT in the United States. Internet exposure of OT and inadequate hardening of remote-access paths were central enabling conditions. The campaign's immediate objective appears to have been disruption of operator visibility/control rather than covert long-term persistence, although persistence cannot be ruled out on the public record. WHAT DO WE SUSPECT? The incidents may be related to the wider pattern of Iranian-affiliated PLC targeting that U.S. agencies warned about in 2023-2026. Common network design or third-party-managed remote connectivity may have amplified impact across multiple victims. WHAT DON'T WE KNOW? Who conducted the Minnesota incidents Whether all incidents were the work of one actor The exact initial access mechanism at each site Which states and utilities outside Minnesota were affected Whether ladder-logic modification caused process manipulation in Minnesota Any full financial, environmental, or long-term recovery impact WHAT EVIDENCE WOULD CHANGE THE ASSESSMENT? Release of authoritative forensic findings from Minnesota, FBI, CISA, or EPA Public IOCs or access logs linking incidents to known actor infrastructure A government attribution statement supported by technical evidence Per-victim incident reports showing whether default credentials, exposed modems, VPNs, or specific CVEs were used Correlated cross-victim evidence demonstrating a single campaign or disproving one Final judgment: The most defensible evidence-based conclusion is that the July 2026 Minnesota incidents and the contemporaneous seven-state activity represent a serious wave of malicious targeting against exposed U.S. water-sector OT, especially PLC-centric remote monitoring/control environments. Public attribution remains unresolved, and physical/public-health consequences in Minnesota are not publicly demonstrated beyond temporary operational disruption and reversion to manual control. Method note: This report prioritized Tier 1 and Tier 2 sources, used Tier 3 sources mainly to identify leads and local impacts, and avoided elevating repeated media claims into independent corroboration where those claims appeared to derive from the same government statements or anonymous-source reporting. Important limitation: Some official local pages were discoverable in search results but not fully retrievable during browsing. Where that occurred, this report either relied on the indexed text itself, secondary reporting that directly quoted the city statement, or marked the issue unresolved rather than inferring missing details.
